question: Why do you want to study Maritime Studies?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific pull toward the maritime industry backed by some real exposure, not a vague love of the sea.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show you understand the industry is about trade and logistics, not just ships
Connect it to what you want from this specific course
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I grew up near a container port and used to watch the ships queue outside the breakwater, and it struck me that almost everything in my house had arrived that way. That curiosity turned serious after I did a week's work placement with a shipping agency, where I saw how much coordination goes into moving one container from a factory to a shelf. I want to study Maritime Studies because it sits at the crossroads of engineering, trade, and law, and I want to understand the whole system, not just the romantic part of it.

commonMistakes: Saying only that they love the sea or love travel
No real exposure to the industry beyond a holiday cruise
Confusing maritime studies with marine biology
followUps: What part of that placement surprised you most?

question: Why do you want to study Maritime Studies at our institution rather than elsewhere?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course, not generic praise that could apply anywhere.

bullets: Name a specific module, simulator, faculty specialism, or industry link
Explain why that feature matters to their own goals
Avoid rankings or prestige as the main reason
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your programme is one of the few that gives students time on a bridge simulator in first year rather than saving practical work for later, and I learn navigation concepts far better hands-on than from a textbook. I also read that your maritime law module is taught by someone who worked in P&I insurance, which is the side of the industry I am most curious about. Between the simulator work and that legal grounding, this course lines up with the kind of well-rounded understanding I want rather than a narrowly technical one.

commonMistakes: Citing only league table ranking
Praise so generic it could fit any maritime school
Not knowing any specific module or facility
followUps: What would you contribute to this course?

question: What first drew you to shipping and the sea, rather than another field?
lookingFor: A believable personal story that shows the interest predates the application, not a line invented for the interview.

bullets: Give a specific, concrete origin, not a vague lifelong claim
Show how the interest developed over time rather than appearing overnight
Tie it to something they actively did, not just watched
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My uncle worked as a chief engineer on bulk carriers, and his stories over dinner about engine rooms and rough Atlantic crossings made the industry feel real rather than abstract. I started reading up on ship types out of curiosity, then joined my school's model boat club where I actually had to think about stability and ballast for the first time. That mix of a personal connection and getting my hands dirty with the actual physics is what turned a passing interest into something I want to build a career on.

commonMistakes: Claiming a lifelong obsession with no specific trigger
Describing only passive interest like watching documentaries
An answer that sounds rehearsed rather than personal
followUps: Has that interest changed or narrowed since then?

question: What relevant experience do you have that connects to maritime studies?
lookingFor: Concrete, reflected-on exposure to the field, whether sailing, work experience, or a related project.

bullets: Describe a specific experience, not a general interest
Explain what they actually learned or noticed from it
Connect it to why the course is the right next step
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spent two summers crewing on a friend's family sailboat, which taught me the basics of reading weather and respecting how quickly conditions change on the water. Last year I also shadowed a port operations manager for three days and saw how a single delayed vessel ripples through berth schedules and trucking arrangements onshore. Both experiences showed me I am drawn to the operational and logistical side of the industry as much as the seamanship itself, which is exactly what I want to study properly.

commonMistakes: Listing experience with no reflection on what it taught them
Overstating minor exposure as deep expertise
No experience at all and no attempt to explain why
followUps: What would you do differently if you repeated that experience?

question: What have you read recently about the shipping or maritime industry?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine, recent engagement with the field beyond the syllabus, with the ability to discuss it critically.

bullets: Name something specific and recent, not a vague genre
Summarise the core argument or finding accurately
Offer their own view or a question it raised
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read a piece in Lloyd's List on the container shipping alliances and how a handful of them now control most of the major east-west trade lanes. What struck me was how little spare capacity that leaves the system when something goes wrong, since so few companies are making coordinated decisions. It made me want to understand the antitrust and regulatory side of shipping alliances, because it feels like an area where the economics and the law are pulling in different directions.

commonMistakes: Naming only a textbook with no independent reading
Vague summary that shows they did not really read it
No opinion or follow-up thought of their own
followUps: Did you agree with the argument it made?

question: A major incident like the Suez Canal blockage disrupts global shipping. Why does one blocked canal matter so much to the world economy?
lookingFor: Understanding of how concentrated global trade routes are and the knock-on effects of a single chokepoint failing.

bullets: Explain why certain canals or straits are chokepoints with few alternatives
Describe the ripple effects on schedules, costs, and inventories
Show awareness this is a live, evolving industry issue
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Canals like Suez exist because sailing around Africa adds roughly a week and significant fuel cost, so an enormous share of Europe-Asia trade funnels through that one narrow passage. When a ship like the Ever Given grounded there, it did not just delay that vessel, it backed up hundreds of others and forced some to reroute entirely, which pushed up freight rates and delayed goods for weeks. It showed me how a system built for efficiency has very little slack, so a localised failure becomes a global one almost overnight.

commonMistakes: Not knowing why the canal matters beyond it being blocked
No mention of downstream effects like costs or delays
Treating it as an isolated event rather than a systemic risk
followUps: What could the industry do to reduce this kind of risk?

question: Roughly how much of world trade by volume moves by sea, and why does shipping dominate?
lookingFor: A roughly accurate figure with a real understanding of why sea freight beats air or land for most goods.

bullets: Give an approximate correct figure, around eighty to ninety percent by volume
Explain the cost-per-tonne advantage over air freight
Note the trade-off of speed versus cost
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Around eighty to ninety percent of world trade by volume travels by sea, because a single large container ship can move tens of thousands of containers at a fraction of the cost per tonne of flying the same goods. Air freight is faster but hugely more expensive, so it tends to get reserved for high-value or time-critical cargo like electronics or pharmaceuticals. For bulk commodities like grain, ore, or oil, and for most manufactured goods, the economics of sea transport are just unbeatable, which is why the whole global economy still runs on ships.

commonMistakes: Giving a wildly inaccurate figure like under fifty percent
Not explaining the cost logic behind sea dominance
Confusing volume share with value share
followUps: Why might value share by sea look different from volume share?

question: Can you explain the difference between a ship's deck department and engine department?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of the basic division of responsibilities aboard a merchant vessel.

bullets: Deck department handles navigation, cargo, and safety on the bridge and above decks
Engine department maintains propulsion, machinery, and power systems below decks
Note both report to the master but run largely separate chains
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The deck department is responsible for navigation, cargo operations, and safety, and it is led by the master through the chief officer and the other deck officers on the bridge. The engine department, led by the chief engineer, keeps the propulsion system, generators, and all the mechanical and electrical systems running, mostly working below decks in the engine room. Both departments answer to the master, but day to day they operate as fairly separate teams with their own watch schedules and specialisms, which is one of the things I find interesting about how a ship actually runs.

commonMistakes: Treating deck and engine as interchangeable roles
Forgetting who each department ultimately reports to
No mention of cargo operations under the deck department
followUps: Which side of that divide interests you more, and why?

question: What is a flag of convenience, and why do shipowners use them?
lookingFor: Understanding of open registries and the commercial and regulatory reasons owners choose them.

bullets: Define a flag of convenience as registering a ship in a country other than the owner's
Give the main motivations: lower cost, lighter tax, easier crewing rules
Acknowledge the criticism around weaker enforcement of labour or safety standards
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A flag of convenience is when a shipowner registers their vessel in a country like Panama or Liberia rather than their own home country, mainly to benefit from lower registration fees, lighter taxation, and more flexible crewing requirements. It is attractive commercially because it can cut operating costs significantly and simplify hiring an international crew. The trade-off that gets criticised is that some open registries have historically been slower to enforce safety and labour standards, which is why port state control inspections exist as a check on that.

commonMistakes: Confusing flag state with the owner's nationality
Only naming the practice without explaining the motivation
Ignoring the safety and labour criticisms entirely
followUps: What is port state control, and how does it address that concern?

question: What is the International Maritime Organization and what does it actually do?
lookingFor: Basic but accurate knowledge of the IMO's role as the UN body setting global shipping standards.

bullets: Identify it as the United Nations agency responsible for shipping safety and environmental standards
Give an example of a convention it produces, like SOLAS or MARPOL
Note it sets standards that member states then enforce through their own law
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The IMO is the United Nations agency responsible for setting global standards for the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping. It produces conventions like SOLAS for safety of life at sea and MARPOL for pollution prevention, which member states then adopt and enforce through their own national law and port inspections. What I find interesting is that the IMO has no ships or enforcement powers of its own, so its real influence comes from getting so many countries to agree on and apply the same rules.

commonMistakes: Confusing the IMO with a national coast guard or navy
Not naming any actual convention it produces
Assuming the IMO can directly enforce rules on ships
followUps: Why might getting global agreement on shipping rules be hard?

question: What does SOLAS stand for and why was it created?
lookingFor: Basic recall of a foundational maritime safety convention and awareness of its origin.

bullets: State it stands for Safety of Life at Sea
Link its origin to the Titanic disaster
Give an example of what it actually regulates, like lifeboats or fire safety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: SOLAS stands for Safety of Life at Sea, and the first version was adopted in 1914 largely in response to the Titanic disaster, which exposed how inadequate lifeboat provision and safety procedures had been. It sets minimum standards for things like the number of lifeboats a ship must carry, fire protection, and navigation equipment. What strikes me is that it has been revised many times since, so it is really a living record of every major lesson the industry has learned the hard way.

commonMistakes: Not knowing what the acronym stands for
No connection made to why it was originally created
Confusing SOLAS with MARPOL or another convention
followUps: Can you name another convention alongside SOLAS?

question: What is the difference between container shipping and bulk shipping, and why does that distinction matter commercially?
lookingFor: Clear understanding of the two dominant cargo models and how their economics and scheduling differ.

bullets: Explain container shipping as standardised boxes on fixed liner schedules
Explain bulk shipping as unpackaged cargo like ore or grain on flexible tramp routes
Note the commercial difference: liner reliability versus tramp market flexibility
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Container shipping moves standardised boxes of manufactured goods on fixed routes and timetables, a bit like a bus service, which makes it predictable but locks operators into running even when demand dips. Bulk shipping carries unpackaged cargo like iron ore, coal, or grain, and it usually operates more like a taxi, chartered for a specific voyage wherever the cargo happens to be. That difference matters commercially because container shipping revenue depends on filling scheduled capacity, while bulk shipping profitability swings much more directly with spot freight rates and global commodity demand.

commonMistakes: Treating all cargo ships as functionally the same
Not distinguishing liner service from tramp trading
Ignoring the commercial or economic implications
followUps: Which of the two do you think is more exposed to economic downturns?

question: What is a ship's draft, and why does it matter to a voyage?
lookingFor: A correct basic definition plus an understanding of its practical operational consequences.

bullets: Define draft as the vertical distance from the waterline to the bottom of the hull
Explain it changes with cargo load and affects which ports or canals the ship can enter
Give a concrete example like a channel or canal depth restriction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A ship's draft is the depth of the hull below the waterline, essentially how far down into the water it sits, and it changes depending on how much cargo, fuel, and ballast the ship is carrying. It matters enormously for route planning because a fully loaded ship might draw too much water to enter a shallow port or transit a canal like the old Panama locks, which forces careful loading decisions. Getting draft calculations wrong is not a minor error either, since running aground because of miscalculated draft can damage the ship and close a waterway for everyone else.

commonMistakes: Confusing draft with a ship's overall height or length
Not connecting it to real operational limits like port depth
Assuming draft is fixed rather than load-dependent
followUps: What other factors besides cargo weight affect draft?

question: Why do piracy hotspots like the Gulf of Guinea or the waters off Somalia persist, and how has the industry responded?
lookingFor: Awareness of the underlying causes of piracy and practical industry countermeasures, not just the headline.

bullets: Link piracy to conditions ashore, such as weak governance or lack of economic opportunity
Describe practical responses like naval patrols, armed guards, and reporting centres
Show awareness the problem shifts location rather than disappearing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Piracy tends to persist where there is weak governance and limited economic opportunity onshore, which is why hotspots like Somalia in the past and the Gulf of Guinea today are both near unstable coastal regions rather than random open ocean. The industry responded off Somalia with coordinated naval patrols, convoy systems, and armed security teams on vessels, which drove incidents down sharply there. What I find interesting is that the problem has not vanished, it has shifted to West Africa, which suggests the root causes onshore still need addressing rather than just policing the water.

commonMistakes: Treating piracy as a purely random criminal act with no context
Naming only military solutions with no mention of root causes
Assuming the problem has been fully solved globally
followUps: What role should shipowners themselves play in prevention?

question: Shipping is under pressure to cut carbon emissions. What are the main challenges to decarbonising the industry?
lookingFor: Balanced understanding of the technical, economic, and regulatory obstacles, not a slogan-level answer.

bullets: Note the scale challenge: ships run for decades and fuel infrastructure is global
Mention alternative fuel options and their current limitations, like cost or availability
Reference regulatory drivers such as IMO targets or the EU emissions trading scheme
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The core challenge is scale and inertia, since ships operate for twenty or thirty years and refuelling infrastructure has to exist consistently at ports worldwide, so you cannot simply swap fuels overnight the way you might update a car. Alternatives like green methanol, ammonia, or hydrogen each solve part of the emissions problem but bring their own issues around cost, energy density, or safe handling on board. The IMO has set emissions reduction targets and regions like the EU are bringing shipping into carbon pricing schemes, which is starting to push owners toward action, but I think the honest answer is that no single fuel has won yet and the industry is placing parallel bets.

commonMistakes: Suggesting a single fuel solves the problem with no trade-offs
Ignoring the infrastructure and fleet-turnover challenge
No mention of any actual regulatory driver
followUps: Which alternative fuel do you think looks most promising, and why?

question: This field offers paths at sea and ashore, from deck officer to port operations to maritime law. Which direction interests you, and why?
lookingFor: A thought-out, realistic sense of direction that still shows openness to what the course will teach.

bullets: Name a genuine current preference with a reason behind it
Show awareness of what that path actually involves day to day
Leave room for the course to change or sharpen that direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I am most drawn to shore-based operations, particularly port and terminal management, because the placement I did showed me how much problem-solving happens in coordinating vessels, cargo, and trucking schedules against constant disruption. I know that is a very different life to going to sea, which is why I am glad this course exposes students to both sides before anyone has to specialise. I am open to that changing once I have had proper exposure to navigation and life aboard, but operations is where my instinct currently points.

commonMistakes: Naming a career path with no reasoning behind it
Sounding completely fixed with no openness to the course shaping their view
Confusing distinct paths, like conflating deck officer training with law
followUps: What do you think you would find hardest about that path?

question: Why is ballast water considered an environmental problem, and how does the industry manage it?
lookingFor: Sound understanding of a less obvious but important environmental issue and its regulatory response.

bullets: Explain ballast water is taken on for stability and can carry organisms between regions
Note the risk of invasive species disrupting ecosystems at the discharge port
Reference the Ballast Water Management Convention and treatment systems
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Ships take on ballast water for stability when they are lightly loaded, and that water often carries small organisms, larvae, or bacteria picked up at the loading port. The problem is that when the ship discharges that water somewhere else entirely, it can release invasive species into an ecosystem with no natural predators, which has caused real ecological damage in places like the Great Lakes. The IMO's Ballast Water Management Convention now requires ships to treat ballast water, using systems like filtration and UV or chemical disinfection, before it is discharged, which is a good example of a problem that is invisible to most people but genuinely reshapes marine ecosystems.

commonMistakes: Not knowing why ballast water is taken on in the first place
Assuming the concern is pollution from oil rather than biological transfer
No awareness of any regulatory or technical response
followUps: Can you name any documented case of ballast-related ecological damage?

question: If a crime is committed on a ship in international waters, whose law applies?
lookingFor: Awareness of flag state jurisdiction and the basic UNCLOS framework, with acknowledgment of its complications.

bullets: State that flag state law generally applies on the high seas
Reference UNCLOS as the framework governing maritime jurisdiction zones
Acknowledge complications such as coastal state powers near shore or crimes involving multiple nationalities
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As a general rule, a ship on the high seas is treated as an extension of its flag state's territory, so the flag state's law and courts have primary jurisdiction, which is set out under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. It gets more complicated in practice, because if the crew, victim, and shipowner are all different nationalities, several states can have a legitimate interest, and coastal states gain more jurisdiction the closer a ship gets to their territorial waters or exclusive economic zone. It is one of the areas where I think the theory is fairly clean but the real cases end up being a genuine puzzle of overlapping claims.

commonMistakes: Assuming no law applies at all on the high seas
Not mentioning UNCLOS or any legal framework
Ignoring the added complexity of mixed nationalities aboard
followUps: How does this change once a ship enters a country's territorial waters?

question: What is your view on autonomous ships? Are they realistic, and what would need to change for them to become common?
lookingFor: A balanced, informed opinion that recognises both the technical progress and the real regulatory and safety barriers.

bullets: Acknowledge real trials and progress, such as short-sea or coastal autonomous vessels
Identify barriers like international law, insurance liability, and cybersecurity
Give a grounded, non-extreme personal view
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think limited autonomy is already realistic, we have seen trials of small autonomous ferries and coastal vessels operate successfully, but I am sceptical about fully unmanned deep-sea container ships becoming common any time soon. A huge barrier is that international law and insurance still assume a master is legally responsible on board, and nobody has fully worked out liability if an unmanned ship causes an accident or gets hacked. My honest view is autonomy will grow gradually from remote monitoring and decision support toward full autonomy, rather than arriving as a sudden switch, because the legal and safety frameworks simply have not caught up yet.

commonMistakes: Either dismissing autonomy entirely or predicting it happens overnight
No mention of legal, liability, or cybersecurity barriers
Treating all levels of autonomy as the same thing
followUps: What role do you think human crew will still play in ten years?

subtopic: Life at sea and its demands
question: Life at sea can mean months away from family in a confined space. How would you cope with that, and have you thought realistically about it?
lookingFor: Honest, realistic engagement with the demands of seafaring rather than a romanticised view.

bullets: Show they have actually spoken to or read about people who do this
Name a realistic personal coping strategy, not a vague reassurance
Acknowledge it is genuinely hard, not dismiss the concern
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spoke to my uncle at length about this, since he did six-month rotations for years, and he was honest that missing birthdays and being seasick in bad weather never fully stopped being hard. What helped him, and what I would lean on too, was building real structure into the routine, keeping a regular exercise habit, and staying disciplined about calling home whenever satellite signal allowed. I am not going to pretend it would be easy, but I would rather go in with clear eyes about that trade-off than discover it is harder than expected once I am already committed to a career at sea.

commonMistakes: Romanticising the lifestyle with no acknowledgment of the difficulty
Giving a vague answer like 'I'll just adapt'
No evidence of having actually researched or spoken to seafarers
followUps: What would make you consider leaving a life at sea for a shore role?

question: During the pandemic, ports around the world saw severe congestion with ships waiting weeks to unload. What caused that, and what did it teach the industry?
lookingFor: Understanding of how demand shocks, labour shortages, and container imbalances combined to cause systemic disruption.

bullets: Identify the surge in consumer goods demand as a trigger
Mention compounding factors like labour shortages and container imbalances
Draw a lesson about resilience or the limits of just-in-time logistics
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The immediate trigger was a sudden surge in demand for goods once lockdowns hit, while people stopped spending on services and started ordering physical products instead, and ports simply were not staffed or resourced for that spike, especially with pandemic-related labour shortages among dockworkers and truckers. Containers also ended up badly out of position, piling up empty in some regions while others faced shortages, which made the whole system less efficient just when it needed to flex the most. The lesson I took from it is that decades of optimising supply chains purely for cost had stripped out the slack needed to absorb a shock, which is part of why companies are now talking seriously about resilience alongside efficiency.

commonMistakes: Blaming congestion on a single simple cause
No mention of labour or container positioning issues
No broader lesson drawn about supply chain design
followUps: Do you think ports are better prepared for a similar shock now?

question: Why do tides matter to a ship's navigator, beyond just the water going up and down?
lookingFor: Practical understanding that tides affect timing, safe passage, and under-keel clearance, not just a textbook definition.

bullets: Explain tides are caused by gravitational pull, mainly from the moon and sun
Connect tides to under-keel clearance in shallow channels or harbours
Note timing a passage around tidal windows, such as entering port at high tide
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Tides happen because of the gravitational pull of the moon, and to a lesser extent the sun, on the oceans, which raises and lowers sea level in a fairly predictable cycle. For a navigator, that matters because a ship with a deep draft might only have enough water under the keel to safely cross a shallow bar or enter a harbour at or near high tide. So passage planning often means timing arrival deliberately around the tidal window, and getting that calculation wrong in a shallow channel is exactly how ships run aground.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the basic cause of tides
Treating tides as irrelevant to modern, powerful ships
No mention of under-keel clearance or passage timing
followUps: How would a navigator find tidal information for a specific port?

question: As a junior officer, you notice the ship is being loaded beyond what you believe is a safe limit, but your senior officer waves it off to save time. What would you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning that takes safety seriously while navigating the real power dynamics of a ship's hierarchy.

bullets: Acknowledge the tension between hierarchy and a genuine safety concern
Describe raising it directly and specifically with the senior officer first
Explain escalating through proper channels if the concern is not resolved
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would not just accept it or stay quiet, because a loading error is not something you get to undo once the ship is at sea in bad weather. I would raise it directly and specifically with the senior officer, showing my actual stability calculations rather than just voicing a vague worry, since a concrete figure is much harder to dismiss than a feeling. If they still waved it off and I genuinely believed the ship was unsafe, I would feel obliged to raise it with the master or through the company's safety reporting system, because going along with something I believe endangers the crew is not a risk I am willing to take just to avoid an awkward conversation.

commonMistakes: Simply deferring to seniority with no pushback at all
Jumping straight to going over someone's head with no attempt to raise it first
Vague answer with no concrete escalation path
followUps: How would you handle it if the senior officer got angry at being challenged?

question: A ship's master has to decide whether to sail on schedule into an approaching storm or delay and risk missing a costly delivery deadline. How should that decision get made?
lookingFor: Sound reasoning that prioritises crew and vessel safety while showing awareness of the commercial pressure involved.

bullets: State clearly that safety of crew and vessel takes priority over schedule
Describe using proper forecasting and routing tools to inform the decision, not guesswork
Acknowledge the real commercial pressure without letting it override safety
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The master's decision has to start from safety, since no delivery deadline is worth risking the crew or the vessel, and that is a principle the whole industry is built around even if it is inconvenient commercially. In practice that means using proper weather routing services and forecast data to assess the storm's real track and intensity, rather than making a judgement call on instinct alone, and building in a safety margin if there is genuine uncertainty. I understand the commercial pressure is real and the master will get questions from the company, but a good master documents the reasoning clearly and stands by a safety-first decision, because that is exactly the kind of judgement the role exists to make.

commonMistakes: Letting commercial pressure override safety in the reasoning
No mention of using actual forecasting or routing tools
Treating it as a simple choice with no acknowledgment of real pressure
followUps: Who else, if anyone, should be involved in that decision?

question: Melting Arctic ice is opening new shipping routes like the Northern Sea Route. What opportunities and risks does that create for the industry?
lookingFor: Awareness of both the commercial appeal and the genuine environmental, safety, and geopolitical complications involved.

bullets: Note the opportunity: significantly shorter Europe-Asia voyages than via Suez
Identify risks such as harsh conditions, limited infrastructure, and ice-strengthened vessel requirements
Mention environmental and geopolitical concerns, including fragile ecosystems and territorial disputes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The Northern Sea Route can cut the distance between Europe and Asia dramatically compared with going via Suez, which is commercially very attractive as ice-free windows get longer each year. But the risks are serious too, ships need ice-class hulls, there is very little search and rescue or salvage infrastructure along the route, and insurance and crewing costs reflect that added danger. I also think the environmental side matters as much as the commercial one, since more traffic through a fragile ecosystem raises real concerns about pollution and disturbance, on top of the fact that Arctic states do not fully agree on the legal status of the route, which makes it as much a geopolitical question as a shipping one.

commonMistakes: Focusing only on the shorter distance with no mention of risk
Ignoring the environmental or geopolitical dimension entirely
Assuming the route is already fully viable year-round
followUps: Which country do you think has the strongest claim over governing that route?
